summary: PAYLOAD ZERO is an interactive web-based spacecraft engineering simulator designed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. Inspired by real mission frameworks like CubeSat 101 and the SmallSat State of the Art (SST-SOA), the game challenges players to balance aerospace trade-offs—mass, power, budget, communication bandwidth, and schedule—across lunar, Martian, and Earth observation missions. Players configure a spacecraft across seven core subsystems and scientific instruments, verify telemetry against strict constraints, fly through simulated mission phases, and navigate real NASA-inspired crisis events (such as solar radiation events and reaction wheel degradation). A post-mission Black Box flight report breaks down engineering decisions, clearly separating verified NASA specifications from game assumptions. By translating space systems engineering into an accessible web experience, PAYLOAD ZERO demonstrates the scientific and logistical compromises behind interplanetary exploration.
details:
# How It Works & Core Architecture

PAYLOAD ZERO is an educational single-page engineering simulator that models the complete life cycle of an unmanned NASA science mission through a four-screen loop:

1. Mission Briefing: Selecting an authentic target (Earth / Landsat 9, Moon / LRO, or Mars / MRO) with binding budget, timeline, radiation, and scientific benchmarks.

2. Spacecraft Builder: An interactive three-column CAD workbench where players configure a launch vehicle, orbit, seven bus subsystems (structure, power array, battery, comms, flight computer, propulsion, and thermal control), and up to four scientific instruments.

3. Live Simulation & Crisis Event: A terminal-style telemetry run through four flight phases, featuring unscripted anomalies inspired by real NASA incidents (such as SOHO solar storms, Kepler reaction wheel failures, and Voyager 2 communication pauses).

4. Black Box Flight Report: Comprehensive post-mission analytics calculating final scores, ranking (S/A/B/C/F), telemetry waterfalls, and causality insights.

# Engineering Trade-Offs & Scientific Modeling

The gameplay is driven by authentic aerospace compromises:

- Propulsion & Mass Multiplication: A target-distance penalty multiplies dry mass by transfer factors (3.0 for Earth, 7.5 for Moon, 16.0 for Mars) to simulate propellant and upper-stage requirements against launcher LEO capacities.

- Solar Irradiance Scaling: At Mars distance, solar generation drops to 43%, necessitating high-efficiency deep-space arrays. Power deficits penalize scientific output by 40%.

- Downlink Bottlenecks: Data rates compete with orbital contact windows. If telemetry generated per day exceeds antenna throughput, science points are permanently throttled.

- Thermal & Radiation Protection: Players must match structural and computing shielding to planetary radiation environments to unlock critical crisis-mitigation options.

# Technology Stack & Implementation

- Pure Vanilla Web: Built with zero runtime dependencies or frameworks using static HTML5, CSS3, and modern Vanilla JavaScript.

- Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG): Procedurally updated CAD blueprint providing real-time visual feedback of installed modules, callouts, and warning pulses.

- Custom Modular Engine: Clean separation of concerns between data (`nasa_data.js`), mathematical logic (`engine.js`), and user interface (`ui.js`).

- Full Bilingual Localization: Built-in internationalization engine (`i18n.js`) with symmetric Ukrainian and English translation dictionaries (670+ keys).

- Open Source Codebase: All code is fully open-source and publicly accessible.

GitHub Repository: [ВСТАВ ТУТ ПОСИЛАННЯ НА ВАШ ВІДКРИТИЙ GITHUB РЕПОЗИТОРІЙ]

# Educational Impact

PAYLOAD ZERO was designed to bridge the gap between academic space system engineering documents (such as NASA CubeSat 101 and SST-SOA) and interactive education. Every item in the catalog explicitly distinguishes verified NASA historical telemetry (marked with ✓) from illustrative gameplay assumptions (marked with ◇), empowering students and space enthusiasts to understand the real compromises behind space mission design.
